code.title: Event loop order: sync, ticks, microtasks, then phases

followUps:
In the poll phase, on the main thread. fs.readFile does the actual disk read on a libuv pool thread; when it finishes, the result is queued and the loop runs your callback during the next poll phase.

So the callback never runs on the worker thread. Any nextTick or promise you schedule inside it runs right after it, and a setImmediate you schedule there runs in the check phase of the same lap, before any setTimeout(0).

It waits (blocks) for I/O, but only as long as it is safe to. If nothing is ready, poll looks at what else is pending: if setImmediate callbacks are queued it moves straight on to the check phase; otherwise it sleeps until the nearest timer is due or an I/O event arrives.

Example: one timer due in 50 ms and no I/O means poll sleeps up to 50 ms using no CPU (via epoll or kqueue), then the loop wraps around to run the timer.

code.title: nextTick vs promises vs setImmediate ordering

followUps:
Because the names describe the wrong thing. nextTick does not wait for the next tick of the loop; it runs before the loop continues. setImmediate does not run immediately; it runs in the check phase, later than a tick.

The names are historical and cannot be changed without breaking old code. Mental model: nextTick means after this operation, Promise.then means after the ticks, setImmediate means after the I/O poll of this lap, setTimeout means at least N ms from now.

Use setImmediate. Process a slice of the work, then schedule the next slice with setImmediate so the loop can handle I/O and timers in between.

function step() {
  doSlice();                  // e.g. 1000 items
  if (more) setImmediate(step);
}

nextTick and promises would not help: they run before the loop moves on, so a long chain still starves I/O. Example: 1,000,000 items in slices of 1,000 give 1,000 yields, each delaying a waiting request by one slice, not the whole job.

The thread libuv uses for the pool: it runs blocking calls that have no non-blocking OS version, so the main thread never waits on them. That covers most fs calls, dns.lookup, crypto.pbkdf2, scrypt, randomBytes and async zlib.

There are 4 threads by default, so only 4 such tasks run at once; the rest queue. Network sockets do not use the pool; they use epoll, kqueue or IOCP directly, which is why thousands of connections are cheap.

Any heavy computation on the main thread. Example: hashing a large upload with a synchronous loop, or running JSON.parse on a 200 MB string takes about 1 second. During that second no other request is read, written or timed, so 5,000 connected clients all freeze at once.

Also bad: a regex with catastrophic backtracking, image resizing in pure JavaScript, or fs.readFileSync in a handler. Move such work to worker threads or another service.

code.title: Blocking loop vs chunked work that yields

followUps:
Measure how late a timer fires compared with when it should have. With perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay() Node records this in a histogram for you.

const h = monitorEventLoopDelay({resolution: 20});
h.enable();
setInterval(() => {
  log(h.percentile(99) / 1e6);  // ms
  h.reset();
}, 5000);

Healthy services show p99 lag of a few ms. If p99 is 400 ms, something blocked the loop for that long. Also check performance.eventLoopUtilization() for how busy the loop is.

Match the pool size to what the work is limited by. For CPU-bound work, use about the number of cores: with 8 cores, 8 workers keep every core busy, and more only adds context switching. For work that mostly waits (I/O), a larger pool helps because threads sleep.

Then verify by load test: raise the size until throughput stops improving. Memory matters too, since each worker thread has its own V8 heap (tens of MB). Start at cores minus 1 and tune with measurements.

code.title: Thread pool queue delays a quick task (simulation)

followUps:
dns.resolve (and its variants like resolve4) does not use the pool. It makes real network DNS queries through the c-ares library, which is asynchronous. dns.lookup uses the system call getaddrinfo, which blocks, so it runs in the pool.

Also, http.get uses dns.lookup by default, so many slow file operations can delay outgoing requests. Using resolve or a DNS cache avoids that.

Because extra threads cost memory and compete for CPU cores and the disk. With 4 cores, a pool of 64 running pbkdf2 gives no more throughput than 4, while each task takes much longer to finish because they share cores, and context switching adds overhead.

For I/O-bound pool work (slow disks, network file systems) a bigger pool helps up to the device limit. Past that it only increases queued memory and latency. Measure, then pick.

code.title: Backpressure: write() false and drain

followUps:
No, it is a soft threshold. write() still accepts data after the buffer passes the mark; it just returns false to tell you to stop. A producer that ignores this keeps filling memory.

Example: highWaterMark of 16 KiB and a 100 KiB write() call: the whole chunk is buffered, the return value is false, and writableLength is 100 KiB. Only the well-behaved producer that waits for 'drain' keeps memory near the mark.

The same way, through the OS. If the client reads slowly, its TCP receive window fills, the server's send buffer fills, and then Node's socket buffer fills, so socket.write() returns false. Pausing the source stops reading from the file, and the source's own OS buffers fill in turn.

So the pressure chain runs from the slow client back to the disk. pipeline() does this wiring for you. Without it, memory per slow client grows with the unsent data.

Use pipeline and listen for failure, because it destroys every stream in the chain when one closes early. When the client disconnects, the response stream closes; pipeline then destroys the file read stream, which closes the file descriptor.

pipeline(fs.createReadStream(p), res, (err) => {
  if (err) log(err.code);  // ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE
});

With plain pipe() the file stream stays open and leaks one descriptor per aborted download, until the process hits its limit (often 1024).

Do not load it with JSON.parse; that needs the whole text in memory (more than 10 GB of heap). Use a streaming parser that emits tokens or items as they arrive, for example a library such as stream-json, inside a pipeline.

Better still, change the format: newline-delimited JSON (one object per line) can be read with readline and parsed line by line, using memory for one record. For example, 50 million lines of 200 bytes each are processed with a few KB of memory in use at once.

code.title: EventEmitter: once wrapper and pitfalls

followUps:
Wrap the listener so it removes itself before it runs, then register the wrapper.

function once(em, name, fn) {
  function w(...a) { em.off(name, w); return fn.apply(this, a); }
  em.on(name, w);
}

Remove first, then call, so that if the listener emits the same event again it does not fire twice. Node's real version also supports off(name, fn) with the original function by storing it on the wrapper (w.listener = fn).

When you want to wait for events with for await instead of nesting callbacks: for await (const [msg] of on(emitter, 'data')) from events. Errors and ending become normal control flow, and the loop gives you natural backpressure, since the next event is handled only when you ask for it.

For a single event use await once(emitter, 'ready'). Use an AbortSignal to stop waiting, otherwise a never-emitted event leaves the code hanging forever.

Run several workers behind the primary and replace them one by one so there is always capacity. With cluster, the primary calls cluster.fork() for a new worker, waits for its 'listening' event, then asks the old worker to disconnect(); it finishes its in-flight requests and exits.

Example with 4 workers: restart them one at a time and the service never drops below 3 workers. Under Kubernetes a rolling update of pods does the same job, and PM2's reload automates the cluster version.

Because a WebSocket handshake takes several HTTP requests in some setups (and Socket.IO's long-polling fallback sends many), and the server keeps per-connection state in one process's memory. If round-robin sends request 2 to a different worker, that worker does not know the session and rejects it.

Sticky sessions (by IP hash or cookie) send one client always to the same worker. Alternatively keep the state in Redis with a pub/sub adapter so any worker can serve it; this is also needed to broadcast to rooms across workers.

code.title: Mini Express middleware chain with error handler

followUps:
The request hangs. If a middleware neither ends the response nor calls next(), Express does nothing else and the client waits until its own timeout, while the connection and the request object stay in memory.

Example: an auth middleware that checks a token, and on success forgets next(): every request to protected routes never gets a reply. The usual rule is that every code path either sends a response or calls next(), and never does both.

compose turns a list of functions into one function, each receiving a next that runs the following one.

function compose(list) {
  return (ctx) => {
    const run = (i) => i === list.length ? undefined
      : list[i](ctx, () => run(i + 1));
    return run(0);
  };
}

This is the idea behind Koa. Each step can do work before and after await next(). It costs O(n) per request for n middleware.

Encapsulation means a plugin and its children get their own scope: decorators, hooks and routes added inside do not leak out to siblings or the parent. Example: an auth plugin adds an onRequest hook; only routes registered inside that plugin are protected, while a sibling /health plugin stays open.

To share something on purpose (a database connection) wrap the plugin with fastify-plugin, which breaks the encapsulation. In Express a global app.use affects everything after it, so the isolation must be built by hand with routers.

Put Fastify in front step by step. Option 1: use @fastify/express (or @fastify/middie) to mount the whole Express app inside Fastify, then rewrite one route at a time as native Fastify routes with schemas.

Option 2: run both and route by path at the proxy (/api/v2 goes to Fastify). Move the shared logic (services, database code) out of the handlers first so both frameworks can call it. Verify each moved route with the same tests and compare latency before and after.

Because after an uncaught exception the process may be in an unknown state: a half-updated object, a lock never released, a connection left open. Carrying on can corrupt data or serve wrong answers while looking healthy.

The safe pattern is to log the error, stop accepting new work, finish or abandon in-flight requests within a short timeout, and exit with a non-zero code so the supervisor (Kubernetes, systemd, PM2) starts a clean process. Running several instances means one restart does not cause an outage.

Stop taking new requests, let current ones finish, release resources, then exit. Steps on SIGTERM: set a flag so the health check fails; call server.close(); wait for connections to end; close the database pool; exit.

process.on('SIGTERM', async () => {
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 25000).unref();
  await new Promise(r => server.close(r));
  await db.end();
  process.exit(0);
});

The forced-exit timer must be shorter than the platform's kill timeout (30 s by default in Kubernetes).

Because server.close() only stops new connections; it completes after every existing connection ends. A keep-alive connection that is idle stays open, and a stuck client can hold one open for minutes, so the callback never fires.

Fix: after calling close(), call server.closeIdleConnections() (Node 18.2+), and after a deadline closeAllConnections(). Also send Connection: close on responses sent during shutdown. WebSockets are never idle-closed, so close them yourself.

The primary process must coordinate the workers. On SIGTERM the primary tells each worker to stop (worker.disconnect()), and each worker runs its own graceful shutdown: close its server, finish requests, exit. The primary exits when all workers are gone.

Watch out for signals: with a process manager the signal may go only to the primary, or to all processes. Under Kubernetes, with one process per pod, none of this is needed; the pod receives the signal directly.

Look at where the waiting happens. Loop blocking: event loop lag is high and CPU is high on the main thread during spikes, and even tiny unrelated requests (a /health check) become slow. Pool starvation: lag stays low, /health is fast, but only requests that use fs, DNS or crypto are slow.

Test: time a trivial fs.stat or crypto.randomBytes in the background. If it takes 500 ms while the loop lag is 2 ms, the pool queue is the problem. Fix it by limiting concurrency or raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE.

Base them on a latency target and on your baseline. A good start: warn when p99 event loop delay stays above 100 ms for 5 minutes; page when it is above 500 ms, or when event loop utilization is above 0.9 for 5 minutes. Add alerts for p99 request latency and for GC pause time.

Use a short window plus a minimum duration so a single brief blip does not wake anyone. Tune after a week using real data: if the p99 is normally 20 ms, a threshold of 100 ms is five times higher than normal.

Give every event an id and let the client reconnect with the standard Last-Event-ID header. The browser's EventSource sends it automatically. The server keeps recent chunks of each response (for example the last 60 seconds in Redis keyed by response id) and replays everything after that id, then continues.

The model call cannot be resumed from the middle, so the server must keep generating without the client (and store the output) or restart. Decide by cost: for short answers regenerating is simpler; for long ones keep the buffer.

Keep a small bounded buffer between the model and the response, and let backpressure do the rest. If res.write() returns false, pause reading from the upstream until 'drain'. Upstream then slows too (its TCP window fills), so memory stays bounded.

Set a limit, for example 1 MB per stream. If the client falls further behind than that, close the stream with an error event and abort the upstream with the AbortController. With 1,000 streams that caps the buffers at about 1 GB, instead of unbounded growth.
